summary: Describes the IP Encapsulating Security Payload, a mechanism that provides integrity and confidentiality for IP datagrams. It is the original ESP specification, later replaced by RFC 2406.

eli5.summary: A locked box for each Internet packet, with a seal that shows if someone has tampered with it.

questions: how does esp encrypt ip packets
how does ip esp differ from authentication header
subtitle: Encrypted packets for secure IP communication.

tldr.problem: IP networks need a way to protect datagram confidentiality and integrity without relying on applications to encrypt data themselves.
tldr.mechanism: The Encapsulating Security Payload adds encryption and optional authentication to IP datagrams, either wrapping entire IP packets (tunnel mode) or just the transport layer payload (transport mode).
tldr.outcome: ESP became a core part of IPsec, though RFC 1827 was replaced by RFC 2406 with refinements. It is largely superseded by modern TLS for application-level encryption and IPsec for VPNs.

today: RFC 1827 is obsoleted by RFC 2406. ESP is a foundational part of IPsec, widely used in VPNs and site-to-site tunnels. Modern applications typically use TLS (RFC 5246, now RFC 8446) for encryption at the application layer instead of IPsec at the network layer.

sections.title: Introduction and Overview
sections.content:
The IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) is a mechanism for protecting IP datagrams with encryption and integrity checking. It may also provide authentication depending on the cryptographic algorithm and mode chosen. ESP works with both IPv4 and IPv6.

ESP does not provide non-repudiation (proof that a specific person sent a message) or protection from traffic analysis (hiding who is talking to whom). For applications needing integrity and authentication without encryption, the IP Authentication Header (AH) is used instead. For defense in depth, AH and ESP can be used together.
sections.eli5: ESP locks up the important parts of a message and adds a security label. You can use it alone, or combine it with another technique called AH for extra security.

sections.title: Two Modes: Tunnel and Transport
sections.content:
ESP has two primary modes of operation, each suited to different scenarios. In Tunnel mode, the entire original IP datagram is encrypted and placed inside a new IP datagram with new unencrypted headers. This mode protects both the data and the fact that the message came from a certain address. In Transport mode, only the transport layer payload (such as TCP or UDP) is encrypted, leaving the original IP headers visible. Transport mode conserves bandwidth because it does not wrap the headers.

A Security Association (SA) identifies which encryption key and algorithm apply to each datagram. The sender uses the destination address and user identity to select the right SA, then applies encryption. The receiver uses the destination address and a 32-bit Security Parameter Index (SPI) to find the matching SA and decrypt the packet.
sections.eli5: Tunnel mode hides the entire message and wraps it in a new envelope; transport mode just locks the payload. Both use a security agreement (SA) to say which key and method to use.

sections.title: ESP Header Structure
sections.content:
The ESP header is assigned Internet Protocol number 50. It consists of an unencrypted header field followed by encrypted data. The unencrypted header contains a 32-bit Security Parameter Index (SPI), which identifies which security association applies to this datagram. Values 0 through 255 are reserved for future use by IANA.

The unencrypted part also contains opaque transform data that depends on the encryption and authentication algorithm in use. The encrypted portion includes protected ESP fields and the user data being secured (either an entire IP datagram in tunnel mode or a transport protocol frame in transport mode). The actual algorithms and formats are defined in separate documents, such as the ESP DES-CBC transform.
sections.eli5: The header starts with a 32-bit label (SPI) that tells the receiver which key to use. Everything after that is locked up using whatever algorithm the security agreement specifies.

sections.title: Processing: Encryption and Decryption
sections.content:
In tunnel mode, the sender takes an IP datagram, encapsulates it into ESP, locates the correct security association based on the destination address and sending user, then encrypts the payload. The encrypted data is placed in a new cleartext IP datagram for transmission. At the receiver, the cleartext IP headers are stripped away, and the combination of the destination address and SPI value locates the decryption key. After decryption, the original IP datagram is extracted and processed normally.

In transport mode, the sender encrypts only the transport-layer frame (TCP, UDP, or ICMP), leaving the original IP headers in the clear. The receiver decrypts using the destination address and SPI, then passes the decrypted transport data to the appropriate application. If no valid security association exists for a packet, the receiver MUST discard it and log the failure to prevent easy-to-exploit denial of service attacks.
sections.eli5: To send: pick a lock (find the SA), seal the message, and send it. To receive: see the label (SPI), unlock it with the right key, and open it.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Limitations
sections.content:
The strength of ESP depends entirely on the quality of the encryption algorithm, the correctness of its implementation, the strength of the key, the security of the key management mechanism, and the correctness of the ESP and IP implementations in all participating systems. If any of these assumptions fail, little real security is provided.

Some cryptographic transforms using block-chaining algorithms without a strong integrity mechanism are vulnerable to cut-and-paste attacks and should not be used unless the Authentication Header is always present. High assurance development techniques are recommended for implementations. Applications should use user-oriented keying rather than host-oriented keying to avoid certain kinds of cryptanalytic attacks on DES and similar algorithms.
sections.eli5: ESP is only as strong as the weakest link: the cipher, the key, the implementation, and the key-keeping system. If you want really safe communication, use both ESP and the Authentication Header together.

fields.desc: Identifies the security association for this datagram.
